title: Michigan Water Blues, Tony Jackson and Emmett Kennedy's blues strains
summary: Who wrote Michigan Water Blues, Tony Jackson's repertoire, and Emmett Kennedy collecting Black songs near Gretna, including Honey Baby.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Where the blues came from: Handy, Bolden and early blues

blocks.x: That's right. Well, did Tony Jackson write Michigan Water? I thought Jelly wrote it.

Well, I don't think Jelly wrote it. He claims, he, I think he admits it was Tony's. He says it was Tony, but Clarence Williams, that's another one he took off. Well, he didn't know it. Always got it. I got a copy of it, published, Michigan Water Blues by Clarence Williams.
Well, I know, but that's just in South.
No, it's not South, but that's,

I think it was Tony's tune. But now, I will have to admit that up to the time I last heard Tony, I heard him play very few Bruce, and I heard him sing no Bruce songs. See, he played some of that kind of music, little snatches of it. But he never, he never sang any Bruce songs. He sang mostly popular songs, and he had a couple of instrumental pieces of his own that he played, probably more than that, but two of them he wrote up and tried to get them published in town and they wouldn't publish them. Offered him $5 for him, which he wouldn't take. But I never heard him use any, any blues songs at all. But he did doubtless know them because everybody around there would know some. Yeah, all right. I knew, I knew certain little strains of blues, although I, I, at first, nobody ever called them blues in the very few days there. Now, Emmett Kennedy that lived in Gretna was a very good musician and used to work in the Chickasaw Cooperage Company where they hired quite a number of Negroes. He would get the Negroes to come over to his little cottage there and he'd take down their songs. See, and he got some songs that, that are, have a blues, have blues strains, sound like it. There's one called Honey Baby, which, which is really a blues, in my estimation, although it's not sixteen bars strictly, you see. But he wrote that and I heard him play it and his niece sang it at a concert in Algiers in 1906. And I know it was, it was current around there and around Gretna before that because my office boy used to sing part of it, just a line or two, you know, and didn't know much. He used to sing little lines from, little lines from a lot of things, you know, see. Why don't you be like me, why don't you be like me, drink good whiskey, boy, let the cocaine be. He would sing that and then he'd say, Don't worry, babe, Papa ain't mad with you. See, and now the funny thing about that is, don't worry, babe, Papa ain't mad with you, but this, this blues that Baby C wrote, he uses that same line in there, see. And I'm sure, I know he was in New Orleans because in 1912 he had a ragtime piece, song, published by Grunewald there, Baby C, see. But he didn't, for some reason or other, he didn't get the blues published there, although it was published the same year, up in, up in, I think it was the same year. I know the blues was 1912, now he was evidently in New Orleans before that anyhow, because he had that one line, Papa ain't mad with you, Honey Baby, Papa ain't mad with you, and this little, this young office boy there at the fertilizer factory, he would sing that, you know, there were different things you know, why don't you be like me, why don't you be like me, get a good high yellow boy and let those black girls be, see, all kinds of trash, you know, that you think about. He was a white boy too, as far as that goes, so I'm sure he got a second hand, he had a couple of brothers that I imagined that taught him or used to sing ahead of me, older brothers, yeah, older brothers that sang, but Kennedy would have these Negroes come in and play, or sing rather, and he'd arrange the stuff, put it on the piano, he was a gifted musician. Who would do that? Emmett Kennedy, his name is, he wrote several books about the people around Gretna, and also two books of what he called mellows, mellows and then more mellows, there were two books came out, and this honey baby is, is, one of the things that I think had bruising, and I had this line in there that also handy used in a way that, oh my honey baby, let's see, oh, central, won't you give me a long distance phone, oh, central, won't you give me a long distance phone, I want to telephone my baby that I'm starting on my journey home,
